places.name: Anne Frank House
places.headline: Sixteen Fifty, Timed Entry Only, and You Must Book Ahead
places.body:
Anne Frank House charges 16.50 euros for adults, 7 euros for visitors aged 10 to 17 and 1 euro for children aged 0 to 9, each figure including a 1 euro booking fee. It opens daily from 9:00.

The single most important practical fact is that entry is by timed online ticket. People still turn up at the door expecting to queue, and that is not how the museum works. Museumkaart and ICOM cardholders still pay the 1 euro booking fee, and the I amsterdam Card gives no discount here.

The museum itself is deliberately austere. There is very little staging, the rooms behind the bookcase are largely empty, and the effect depends on that emptiness. It is the least theatrical major museum in the city and by some distance the most affecting.
places.what_great: The price is low for what it is, and the child and youth rates are genuinely cheap. The presentation is restrained and trusts the material rather than dramatising it. Opening from 9:00 daily gives an early slot that is quieter and, for this particular site, considerably better.
places.what_ruined: You cannot simply turn up: entry is timed and online, and slots go quickly. The I amsterdam Card gives no discount, and even Museumkaart and ICOM holders pay the 1 euro booking fee. The house is small and the staircases are steep and narrow, which constrains both pace and access.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. The price is modest, the site is handled with restraint rather than spectacle, and the only real barrier is that you must book ahead, which is a planning issue rather than a value one.
places.meta_description: Anne Frank House costs 16.50 euros for adults including the booking fee, 7 euros for ages 10 to 17. Booking ahead is not optional.

places.what_it_is: The canal house on the Prinsengracht where Anne Frank and seven others hid from 1942 to 1944, preserved with the annexe behind the bookcase, alongside a museum built around the diary and the events surrounding it.
places.why_go: Because the rooms themselves do something no book or film manages. The scale of the hiding place, and how ordinary the building is from the street, is the part that stays with people.
places.the_good: Modest pricing for a site of this significance, with 7 euros for ages 10 to 17. The curation is restrained and the empty rooms are left to speak. The 9:00 opening gives a genuinely quieter slot for a visit that benefits from quiet.
places.the_downsides: Timed online booking is mandatory and slots sell out, which turns a spontaneous visit into a closed door. The I amsterdam Card is not accepted for a discount. The house is physically tight, with steep narrow stairs, and busy slots feel crowded quickly.
places.best_for: Essentially every visitor to Amsterdam, and particularly anyone travelling with teenagers, for whom the 7 euro rate and the subject matter combine well.
places.skip_if: You have not booked and are leaving tomorrow, because there is no walk-up option. Consider skipping if you are travelling with young children, since the subject is heavy and the stairs are difficult for small legs.
places.practical: Book online as far ahead as you can manage; this is the one Amsterdam attraction where leaving it to the day will simply fail. Take an early slot. Expect steep stairs and pack light, because the annexe is not a place to be carrying a large bag.
places.tickets: Adults pay 16.50 euros, ages 10 to 17 pay 7 euros and ages 0 to 9 pay 1 euro, each including a 1 euro booking fee. Museumkaart and ICOM cardholders pay the 1 euro booking fee, an EYC card is 7 euros, and the I amsterdam Card gives no discount. Entry is by timed online ticket only.
places.getting_there: Tram 13, 17 or 19 to Westermarkt puts you a minute away. It is around a twenty-minute walk from Amsterdam Centraal along the canals, which is a pleasant approach in its own right.
places.location_context: On the Prinsengracht in the Jordaan, beside the Westerkerk, in the canal belt west of the centre. The Jordaan is one of the most attractive districts in the city and worth walking either side of your slot.
places.time_needed: About ninety minutes, including the museum section after the annexe. It is not a visit to rush and the routing does not encourage rushing.
places.accessibility: The historic house has steep, narrow staircases and is difficult or impossible for visitors with reduced mobility; the museum publishes accessibility guidance and it should be checked before booking.
places.verdict: The most important thing to see in Amsterdam and one of the least expensive. Book it before you book anything else on your trip, take the earliest slot you can, and do not count on the I amsterdam Card helping you here.

places.name: Rijksmuseum
places.headline: Twenty-Five Euros, Free Under 18, and the Only Dutch Museum You Cannot Skip
places.body:
The Rijksmuseum charges 25 euros for adults, with free admission for visitors up to 18 years old. For a national collection of this size that is reasonable, and the under-18 policy makes a family visit dramatically cheaper than the equivalent in Paris or London.

The building reopened in 2013 after a decade-long renovation and it shows: the layout is clear, the lighting is good, and the Gallery of Honour funnels you toward the Dutch Golden Age painting that most people come for.

That funnel is also the problem. The crowd concentrates hard around a handful of Rembrandts and Vermeers, while rooms of equally good seventeenth-century work sit half empty a few metres away.
places.what_great: The collection is the definitive account of Dutch art and it is presented in a building that was rebuilt specifically to show it well. Free admission for everyone up to 18 is genuinely generous. Four Van Gogh paintings including a famous self-portrait are here, which surprises people who assume they are all at the Van Gogh Museum.
places.what_ruined: The Gallery of Honour and the room around The Night Watch are congested for most of the day, and that is where nearly everyone spends their time. Twenty-five euros is real money if you are also doing the Van Gogh Museum and Anne Frank House in the same trip, which most visitors are.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the collection and the building. Value is four because 25 euros is fair for what is here, and under-18s go free, which materially changes the cost of a family visit.
places.meta_description: The Rijksmuseum costs 25 euros for adults and is free for under-18s. What to see, when to go, and why the crowd concentrates in one room.

places.what_it_is: The Dutch national museum, in a purpose-built 1885 Cuypers building on the Museumplein, covering Dutch art and history with the seventeenth-century Golden Age collection at its centre.
places.why_go: Because this is where the Dutch Golden Age is properly explained rather than sampled, and because the post-renovation building is one of the best museum interiors in Europe.
places.the_good: A definitive collection in a building rebuilt to display it, clear routing, and free entry for everyone up to 18. It also holds four Van Gogh paintings, so a visitor short on time gets some of that story here too.
places.the_downsides: The crowd concentrates almost entirely in the Gallery of Honour, which makes the headline paintings the least comfortable part of the museum. At 25 euros it is the most expensive of Amsterdam's three essential museums, and most visitors are paying for all three.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in art or Dutch history, families given the free under-18 entry, and first-time visitors to Amsterdam who only have room for one museum.
places.skip_if: You have a single day and a stronger interest in Van Gogh specifically, in which case the Van Gogh Museum next door is the better use of the time and 25 euros.
places.practical: Start at the far end of the collection and work back toward the Gallery of Honour, which reverses the standard flow and puts you in the busiest room when everyone else has already left it. Book online for a timed slot. The museum sits on the Museumplein alongside the Van Gogh Museum, so the two combine without any travel.
places.tickets: Adults pay 25 euros. Admission is free for visitors up to 18 years old. Tickets are timed and are best booked in advance through the museum's own site.
places.getting_there: Tram 2 or 12 to Rijksmuseum, or tram 5 to Museumplein. It is a walk of roughly twenty minutes from Amsterdam Centraal, or a short ride on tram 2.
places.location_context: On the Museumplein in Amsterdam Zuid, sharing the square with the Van Gogh Museum and the Concertgebouw. This is a calm, green, well-off part of the city and a considerable contrast to the canal belt.
places.time_needed: Two to three hours. The Golden Age floor alone is a solid ninety minutes if you are interested in it.
places.accessibility: The building was comprehensively renovated and reopened in 2013 with lift access throughout, and the museum publishes detailed accessibility information for visitors.
places.verdict: The one Amsterdam museum that is hard to argue with. Book a slot, walk the collection backwards to dodge the crush, and take advantage of the free under-18 entry if you are travelling with family.

places.name: Stedelijk Museum
places.headline: The Modern One on Museumplein, and the Quietest of the Three
places.body:
The Stedelijk charges 22,50 euros for adults and 12,50 for students and CJP holders, with free entry for visitors under 19. It opens 10am to 6pm daily, with no entry after 5.45pm.

It is the third museum on the Museumplein and the one most visitors drop when their schedule tightens. That is exactly why it is worth keeping: the Rijksmuseum and the Van Gogh Museum are both excellent and both crowded, while the Stedelijk holds modern and contemporary art in rooms where you can stand still.

The building is two halves, a nineteenth-century original and a white extension universally known as the bathtub. Opinions on it are strong in both directions, which is more than most museum architecture manages.
places.what_great: Modern and contemporary art of real quality with room to actually look at it, which neither of its neighbours can offer. Slightly cheaper than the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum, free for under-19s, and half price for students. Same square, so it costs nothing in travel time.
places.what_ruined: It is the least essential of the three Museumplein museums if you only have time for one, and it knows it. The 5.45pm cut-off catches late arrivals who assume a 6pm close means 6pm entry. The extension divides opinion sharply enough that some visitors dislike the building itself.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the collection is strong and the building is interesting, without quite the singular pull of its two neighbours. Value is four: 22,50 euros is slightly less than the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh, and it is far less crowded.
places.meta_description: The Stedelijk costs 22,50 euros, 12,50 for students and free under 19. The third museum on Museumplein, and the one with space to think.

places.what_it_is: Amsterdam's museum of modern and contemporary art and design on the Museumplein, in a nineteenth-century building joined to a large white extension completed in 2012.
places.why_go: For twentieth-century and contemporary work seen in comfort, and for a collection that includes design and applied art alongside painting. It is the counterweight to the Golden Age and Van Gogh story the other two tell.
places.the_good: Noticeably quieter than its neighbours, slightly cheaper at 22,50 euros, free under 19 and 12,50 for students and CJP holders. Sharing the Museumplein with the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum means no travel between them.
places.the_downsides: If you can only do one Museumplein museum, this is not it, and the museum competes directly with two more famous neighbours. No entry after 5.45pm despite a 6pm close. The extension is genuinely divisive architecture.
places.best_for: Visitors staying long enough to do more than one museum, anyone interested in modern design as well as art, students on the 12,50 rate and families given free under-19 entry.
places.skip_if: You have one museum slot in Amsterdam. Take the Rijksmuseum, or the Van Gogh Museum if he is the draw. The Stedelijk is the third visit, not the first.
places.practical: Arrive before 5.45pm or you will not get in regardless of the 6pm closing time. Pair it with the Rijksmuseum or Van Gogh Museum on the same square, ideally with this one second when the others have worn you out and you want somewhere calm.
places.tickets: Adults pay 22,50 euros and students and CJP holders pay 12,50 euros. Visitors under 19 go free, as do Stedelijk members. Open daily 10am to 6pm with no entry after 5.45pm.
places.getting_there: Tram 2 or 12 to Rijksmuseum, or tram 5 to Museumplein, both on the same square. Roughly twenty-five minutes on foot from Amsterdam Centraal.
places.location_context: Museumplein 10 in Amsterdam Zuid, on the same square as the Rijksmuseum, the Van Gogh Museum and the Concertgebouw, in a quiet and well-off part of the city away from the canal-belt crowds.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours. It is comfortably done in an afternoon alongside one of its neighbours.
places.accessibility: The museum is served by lifts across both buildings and publishes accessibility information for visitors with reduced mobility.
places.verdict: The Museumplein museum people skip and should not, provided it is your second or third rather than your only one. Go late in the day for the quiet, but be through the door before 5.45pm.

places.name: Van Gogh Museum
places.headline: Twenty-Five Euros, Sixteen for Students, and Buy Only From the Official Site
places.body:
The Van Gogh Museum charges 25 euros per person, with students at 16 euros on presentation of a student card and free admission for visitors under 18.

The museum is unusually direct about one thing, and it is worth repeating: buy from the official site or its named official resellers, because other platforms may offer fraudulent tickets. This is not a general caution about markups, it is the museum warning that tickets bought elsewhere may not work.

The collection is the largest of Van Gogh's work anywhere, arranged broadly chronologically, and the effect of walking a single artist's development from the dark early Dutch work to the last French paintings is something no mixed collection can reproduce.
places.what_great: The largest Van Gogh collection in the world, arranged so the artist's development is legible rather than just displayed. Students pay 16 euros and under-18s are free. It sits on the Museumplein directly beside the Rijksmuseum, so the two need no travel between them.
places.what_ruined: The building is small relative to the ticket price and the visit is correspondingly short. Timed slots sell out well ahead in high season. The official warning about fraudulent tickets on unofficial platforms is a real risk that catches visitors out every year.
places.rating_rationale: Five because it is the definitive collection of one of the most important painters who ever lived. Value is four: 25 euros is fair, but the museum is small enough that the visit is short.
places.meta_description: The Van Gogh Museum costs 25 euros, 16 for students and free under 18. Why buying anywhere except the official site is a genuine risk.

places.what_it_is: A museum on the Museumplein holding the world's largest collection of Van Gogh's paintings, drawings and letters, built around the collection kept by the artist's brother Theo and his family.
places.why_go: Because seeing one artist's entire arc in order, in one building, changes how you read the famous paintings. The late work lands very differently once you have walked through the decade that preceded it.
places.the_good: Unmatched depth on a single major artist, clear chronological presentation, students at 16 euros and under-18s free. The letters displayed alongside the paintings are the part most visitors do not expect and remember most.
places.the_downsides: It is a small museum for 25 euros and you may be out in ninety minutes. Timed slots sell out in advance. Tickets bought outside the official site and its named resellers may be fraudulent, which is a harsher failure mode than simply overpaying.
places.best_for: Anyone with any interest in Van Gogh or in nineteenth-century painting, students given the reduced rate, and visitors who prefer a focused museum to an encyclopaedic one.
places.skip_if: You have one museum slot in Amsterdam and a broader interest in art or Dutch history, in which case the Rijksmuseum covers more ground for the same money.
places.practical: Book directly at the museum's own ticketing site well in advance, and treat any other platform with suspicion unless it is one the museum names. Combine it with the Rijksmuseum on the same square. Go late in the day if you want the last rooms to yourself.
places.tickets: Adults pay 25 euros, visitors under 18 are free, and students pay 16 euros on presentation of a student card. The museum warns that platforms other than its official site and named official resellers may offer fraudulent tickets.
places.getting_there: Tram 2 or 12 to Rijksmuseum or tram 5 to Museumplein puts you on the same square. It is around twenty-five minutes on foot from Amsterdam Centraal.
places.location_context: On the Museumplein in Amsterdam Zuid, next to the Rijksmuseum and the Concertgebouw, in a quiet and affluent part of the city well away from the canal-belt crowds.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours. It is a focused museum and most people see all of it comfortably in that time.
places.accessibility: The museum is served by lifts across its floors and publishes accessibility information for visitors with reduced mobility.
places.verdict: Essential if Van Gogh means anything to you at all, and still very good if he does not. Book direct, ignore third-party ticket sites the museum has not named, and pair it with the Rijksmuseum next door.

places.name: Acropolis Museum
places.headline: Twenty Euros for the Parthenon Marbles, and the Argument About the Missing Half
places.body:
The Acropolis Museum charges 20 euros general admission and 10 euros reduced. Those are the summer rates, running 1 April to 31 October; the winter season from 1 November to 31 March is cheaper at 15,00 euros general, with the reduced rate staying at 10,00.

The museum was built to make a point. The top floor, the Parthenon Gallery, is oriented on exactly the same axis as the Parthenon itself, which stands visible through the glass a few hundred metres uphill. The surviving sculptures are mounted at their original spacing and height. Where a piece is in London rather than Athens, a plain white cast stands in its place.

Walking that colonnade, with the original building in the window and the gaps marked in blank plaster, is the most effective argument in the Elgin Marbles dispute that either side has made. You are not told what to think; you are shown the holes.
places.what_great: The Parthenon Gallery is a genuinely brilliant piece of museum design, and the sightline to the actual Parthenon through the glass does work no label could. The excavated ancient neighbourhood under the glass floor at the entrance is included. Winter admission drops to 15 euros, and there are several free admission days each year.
places.what_ruined: Twenty euros is on top of the separate ticket for the Acropolis itself, so seeing both is a real outlay. The building is busy from mid-morning through the afternoon in season. The reduced rate stays at 10 euros in winter while the general rate falls, which narrows the concession when the museum is quietest.
places.rating_rationale: Five because the top-floor Parthenon Gallery is one of the most intelligent museum spaces built this century. Value is four: 20 euros in summer, dropping to 15 in winter, with a 10 euro reduced rate.
places.meta_description: The Acropolis Museum costs 20 euros general admission and 10 reduced, with a lower winter rate. Why the top floor is the whole point.

places.what_it_is: A purpose-built museum at the foot of the Acropolis, opened in 2009, holding the finds from the Acropolis slopes and summit, with a top-floor gallery displaying the surviving Parthenon frieze and metopes in their original arrangement.
places.why_go: For the Parthenon Gallery, which aligns with the real building visible through the window and marks every absent sculpture with a blank cast. It is the clearest presentation of a contested collection anywhere.
places.the_good: Exceptional museum architecture that argues through arrangement rather than text. The glass floor over the excavated ancient neighbourhood is included at the entrance. Winter admission falls to 15,00 euros, and the museum runs free admission days including 6 March and 25 March.
places.the_downsides: It is a second ticket on top of the Acropolis site itself. Peak season crowds build from mid-morning. The reduced rate does not fall in winter even though the general rate does.
places.best_for: Anyone visiting the Acropolis, which is effectively everyone in Athens, and particularly visitors interested in the Parthenon Marbles question who want to see how the case is actually made.
places.skip_if: You have half a day in Athens and have not yet been up to the Acropolis itself. The site comes first; this is the companion to it, not a substitute.
places.practical: Go early or late in the day in summer. Do the Acropolis first and the museum second, because the gallery makes far more sense once you have stood on the hill. If your dates are flexible, the winter season from 1 November is 5 euros cheaper and considerably quieter.
places.tickets: General admission is 20 euros with reduced admission at 10 euros in the summer season, 1 April to 31 October. In the winter season, 1 November to 31 March, general admission is 15,00 euros and reduced stays at 10,00 euros. Reduced and free tickets are obtained through specific channels rather than the general desk, and there are free admission days including 6 March and 25 March.
places.getting_there: Akropoli station on Metro line 2 is directly outside the entrance. It is a short walk from the Plaka and from the pedestrianised Dionysiou Areopagitou street that runs below the Acropolis.
places.location_context: Makrygianni, immediately south-east of the Acropolis rock, on the pedestrian street that circles the base of the hill. Plaka and Monastiraki are within fifteen minutes on foot.
places.time_needed: Two hours. The Parthenon Gallery alone deserves forty-five minutes, and the ground-floor excavation is worth stopping for on the way in.
places.accessibility: The museum is step-free with lifts to all levels, which is a marked contrast to the Acropolis site itself.
places.verdict: Go, and go after you have climbed the hill rather than before. Twenty euros is fair for what is one of the best museum buildings of the century, and if you can travel in the winter season it is 15.

places.name: Acropolis of Athens
places.headline: Thirty Euros Now, and the Only Real Decision Is What Time You Climb
places.body:
A ticket to visit the Acropolis of Athens is 30,00 euros through the official Hellenic Heritage ticket store.

That is the headline, but it is not the decision that will determine whether you enjoy this. The hour you go is. The rock is bare limestone with almost no shade, the marble underfoot is polished slick by two and a half thousand years of feet, and in July and August the site regularly closes in the middle of the day when temperatures make it unsafe. People who book a midday slot in summer are the ones who come away saying it was overrated.

Go at opening, or in the last two hours before close. The light is better at both ends, the crowd is thinner, and you will actually be able to stand and look at the Parthenon rather than shuffling past it looking for shade.
places.what_great: It is the single most consequential building in Western architecture and you can walk up to it. The site includes the Propylaia, the Erechtheion with its caryatid porch, the Temple of Athena Nike and the theatres on the southern slope, so one ticket covers a great deal. Early and late slots are genuinely pleasant.
places.what_ruined: Thirty euros is a significant increase on the historic price and there is a further ticket if you want the Acropolis Museum below. There is essentially no shade on the summit. Midday closures in summer heat are real and can remove your slot. The polished marble is slippery in any weather.
places.rating_rationale: Five because it is the Acropolis and nothing substitutes for standing on it. Value is four rather than five: 30 euros is a substantial rise from what this cost a few years ago, and the summer heat can take the visit away from you entirely.
places.meta_description: The Acropolis of Athens costs 30 euros through the official ticket store. Why the hour you go matters more than anything else you decide.

places.what_it_is: The citadel rock above Athens, holding the Parthenon, the Erechtheion, the Temple of Athena Nike and the Propylaia, together with the southern slope sites including the Theatre of Dionysus and the Odeon of Herodes Atticus.
places.why_go: Because the Parthenon is the reference point for two thousand years of Western building and photographs consistently fail at the one thing that matters, which is how the proportions behave as you move around it.
places.the_good: One ticket covers the summit and the slope sites, which is more than most visitors realise. The Erechtheion's caryatid porch rewards a long look. Early morning and late afternoon are genuinely calm, and the view over Athens to the sea is worth the climb on its own.
places.the_downsides: Thirty euros, and the Acropolis Museum below is a separate ticket. No shade at the top. Summer midday closures for heat are a real risk to a booked slot. The marble walkways are slippery and the climb is unsuitable for some visitors.
places.best_for: Every first-time visitor to Athens. Also anyone who can be at the gate for opening, since that is when the site is at its best by a wide margin.
places.skip_if: You cannot manage uneven, slippery stone on a gradient, in which case the Acropolis Museum below tells much of the story with lifts and level floors. Skip a midday summer slot in particular, rather than skipping the site.
places.practical: Book the earliest slot available, or the last two hours. Take water and a hat; there is no shade. Wear shoes with grip, because the marble is polished. Do the summit first and the southern slope on the way down. Check for heat closures on the day in July and August.
places.tickets: A visit to the Acropolis of Athens is 30,00 euros through the official Hellenic Heritage ticket store, with timed entry required. Reduced and free tickets require valid ID or documentation at entry. The Acropolis Museum is a separate ticket.
places.getting_there: Akropoli station on Metro line 2 for the southern slope entrance, or Monastiraki on lines 1 and 3 for the approach through Plaka. The main entrance is on the western side above the Areopagus.
places.location_context: The rock rises directly above the centre of Athens, with Plaka on its northern slopes, the Acropolis Museum immediately south-east, and the Ancient Agora below to the north-west.
places.time_needed: Two hours for the summit and the southern slope at a reasonable pace. Three if you take the theatres properly.
places.accessibility: There is a lift on the northern side for visitors with reduced mobility, but the summit surfaces are uneven polished marble and the site is demanding; the Acropolis Museum below is fully step-free by contrast.
places.verdict: Unmissable, and the only thing you really need to get right is the hour. Book the first slot of the day, carry water, and treat a midday summer booking as the one genuine mistake available here.

places.name: National Archaeological Museum
places.headline: Twenty Euros for the Best Greek Collection on Earth, and Half of Athens Walks Past It
places.body:
A ticket to visit the National Archaeological Museum is 20,00 euros through the official Hellenic Heritage ticket store.

This is the best collection of ancient Greek material in the world, and a large share of visitors to Athens never go, because it sits in Exarcheia rather than in Plaka and does not appear on the walk between the Acropolis and the Agora.

What is inside: the gold Mask of Agamemnon and the Mycenaean shaft grave finds, the bronze Artemision Zeus or Poseidon caught mid-throw, the Jockey of Artemision, the Antikythera Mechanism, and a sculpture collection that runs the whole arc from Cycladic figurines to Roman portraiture. The Antikythera Mechanism alone, a geared bronze astronomical calculator from the second century BC, rewrites what most people assume about ancient technology.
places.what_great: The collection has no rival for ancient Greek material and it is presented with room to breathe. Twenty euros is fair for its scale. It is markedly quieter than the Acropolis, so you can stand in front of the Mycenaean gold without being moved along.
places.what_ruined: It is a twenty-minute walk from the Plaka in a workaday part of the city, which is why so many visitors skip it. The building is large and the labelling is uneven, so some outstanding objects are easy to walk past. There is no natural pairing nearby, so it needs its own half-day.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. It holds the finest collection of ancient Greek art anywhere, it costs 20 euros, and it is consistently far quieter than the Acropolis sites because it sits outside the tourist quarter.
places.meta_description: The National Archaeological Museum costs 20 euros. The Mask of Agamemnon, the Antikythera Mechanism, and far fewer people than the Acropolis.

places.what_it_is: Greece's national archaeological collection, in a nineteenth-century neoclassical building in Exarcheia, covering prehistoric, Mycenaean, Cycladic, sculpture, bronze, pottery and Egyptian collections.
places.why_go: For the Mycenaean gold, the Artemision bronzes and the Antikythera Mechanism. These are the objects that other museums borrow, and they are all in one building.
places.the_good: The finest ancient Greek collection anywhere, at 20 euros, with far fewer people than the Acropolis sites. The bronzes in particular are displayed with enough space to walk around them, which is rarely true elsewhere.
places.the_downsides: Outside the tourist quarter, so it takes a deliberate trip. Uneven labelling means significant objects can go unnoticed. Its scale is tiring and there is nothing else nearby to build a day around.
places.best_for: Anyone with a real interest in the ancient world, repeat visitors to Athens, and travellers who prefer a quiet museum to a crowded monument.
places.skip_if: You have one day in Athens. The Acropolis and its museum come first. This is the second-day museum, and it deserves to be treated as one rather than squeezed in.
places.practical: Give it a half-day and go straight to the Mycenaean room and the bronzes before fatigue sets in. It is about twenty-five minutes on foot from Syntagma, or take the metro to Omonia and walk. Exarcheia is fine by day and has good, cheap places to eat.

places.verdict: The most underrated major museum in Europe and the best value in Athens. Go on your second day, head for the bronzes and the Mycenaean gold first, and allow more time than you planned.

places.name: Basilica de la Sagrada Familia
places.headline: Finished at Last, and Priced Like It Knows
places.body:
The argument for going changed in 2026. After more than 140 years the basilica reached its final height of 172.5 metres when the upper arm of the cross on the central Tower of Jesus Christ was installed on 20 February 2026, making it the tallest church in the world, past Ulm Minster's roughly 162 metres in October 2025.

What you queue for is no longer a building site with a good gift shop. It is a completed exterior.

The price has moved with the fame. General entry is 26,00 euros at the official box office and 36,00 with tower access. Seniors pay 21,00 and 28,00, and under-30s and student card holders pay 24,00 and 34,00. Disabled visitors and their companions pay only for additional services, with general entrance free.
places.what_great: It is finished, and the difference is visible from the street. The interior light through the nave columns is why the building survives its own crowds, and the tower climb is the only way to see detail Gaudi put where he assumed nobody would stand. The official site sells direct, so there is no reason to pay a reseller.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-six euros is the entry, not the total: towers are ten more and a guided tour is 30. Timed entry means a missed slot is a missed visit. Resellers dominate search results and quote well above the official rate for the same ticket, so people routinely pay a premium for nothing at all.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the thing itself, which is now a completed world record rather than a building site. Value drops to three because 26 euros before towers is high for a single building and the reseller market pushes many visitors above that for nothing.

places.name: La Pedrera (Casa Mila)
places.headline: From Twenty-Nine Euros, and the Roof Is the Whole Point
places.body:
La Pedrera, properly Casa Mila, charges from 29 euros for the essential general admission and from 25 euros for the sunset slot.

The building is Gaudi's last civil work, a stone apartment block with no straight structural walls and a roof terrace of chimneys that look like helmeted sentries. The roof is the reason to go. The rest of the visit, an apartment furnished as it would have been in the 1910s and an attic of parabolic brick arches, is good, but the roof is what people remember.

The sunset ticket is cheaper than the standard one, which is unusual, and puts you on that roof at the best hour of the day. If your schedule allows it, that is the ticket to buy.
places.what_great: The roof terrace is one of the great built spaces in Barcelona and the attic's brick arches explain how the building stands up. The sunset slot costs less than standard admission, which is a rare case of the better experience also being the cheaper one.
places.what_ruined: From 29 euros is a lot for a single apartment building, especially if you are also paying for Sagrada Familia and Park Guell on the same trip. The route is one-way and the roof is small, so a full slot feels full. The Passeig de Gracia frontage is permanently crowded with people photographing it for free.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the roof terrace is among the best things Gaudi built and the apartment reconstruction is genuinely informative. Value is three: from 29 euros for one building is steep even by Barcelona standards.

places.name: MACBA
places.headline: Fifteen Euros Inside, and the Best Free Show Is on the Plaza Outside
places.body:
MACBA charges 15,00 euros for a general admission entry ticket bought at the reception desk, and 13,50 euros for the same ticket bought online.

The museum is Richard Meier's white modernist block dropped into the Raval, one of the densest and most working-class quarters of the old city, and that collision is a large part of what the building means. The collection concentrates on Catalan and Spanish art from the mid-twentieth century onward, with strong holdings in conceptual and post-conceptual work.

The plaza outside is the part that made it internationally famous, and not for the art. Placa dels Angels has been one of the most filmed skate spots in the world for three decades. It costs nothing, it runs all day, and for a lot of visitors it is the better show.
places.what_great: A serious contemporary collection with real depth in Catalan and Spanish art, in a Meier building worth seeing on its own. Booking online saves 1,50 euros. The plaza outside is free, permanently busy with skaters, and one of the genuinely characterful public spaces in the city.
places.what_ruined: Contemporary art is divisive and this collection makes few concessions to visitors who are not already interested. Fifteen euros at the desk is avoidable by booking online, which not everyone realises. The Raval immediately around it is lively but noticeably rougher at night than the Gothic Quarter.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the collection is strong on Catalan and Spanish contemporary work and the Meier building is a landmark in its own right. Value is four: 15 euros at the desk, 13,50 online.
places.meta_description: MACBA costs 15 euros at the desk or 13.50 online. Barcelona's contemporary art museum, and the skate plaza that made it famous.

places.name: Berlinische Galerie
places.headline: Seven Euros on the First Wednesday, Free Under Eighteen, and Berlin's Own Art
places.body:
The Berlinische Galerie offers reduced admission of 7 euros for all on the first Wednesday of every month, free admission for under 18s, and free admission for refugees.

The collection is deliberately local. This is art made in Berlin from 1870 onward, which means the Secession, Dada, New Objectivity, the divided city and what came after reunification. It is the story of one city told through the art it produced, rather than a survey assembled from elsewhere.

That focus is the appeal and the limitation. If you want a broad museum this is the wrong one, and the Gemaldegalerie or the Neue Nationalgalerie will suit you better. If you want to understand why Berlin looks and behaves the way it does, this is the more useful hour.
places.what_great: Reduced 7 euro admission for everyone on the first Wednesday of each month, free for under 18s and free for refugees, which is an unusually broad set of concessions. The building is a converted glass warehouse with generous, well-lit space, and the Berlin-specific focus makes it genuinely different from the national collections.
places.what_ruined: The collection is narrow by design, so visitors expecting a general modern art museum can find it thin. The first Wednesday is correspondingly busy. It sits in Kreuzberg away from the Museum Island cluster, so it needs a deliberate trip.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the collection is narrower than the big national museums, which suits some visitors and not others. Value is five: reduced admission on the first Wednesday of the month, free for under 18s and free for refugees.

places.name: Jewish Museum Berlin
places.headline: The Core Exhibition Is Free, and the Building Is Half the Argument
places.body:
Admission to the core exhibition at the Jewish Museum Berlin is free of charge for everyone. That is unusual for a museum of this scale and it removes the main reason people talk themselves out of going.

The building is by Daniel Libeskind and it is not a container for the exhibition, it is part of it. Sharp angles, slanting floors, voids cut through the full height of the structure and a Holocaust Tower that is an unheated concrete shaft with a single slit of daylight. Whether that architecture is moving or manipulative is an argument people have, and having the argument is part of visiting.

The core exhibition itself covers two millennia of German Jewish life, and is careful to be a history of a people rather than only a history of their destruction.
places.what_great: The core exhibition is free for everyone, which for a national-scale museum is remarkable. It tells German Jewish history as a whole rather than collapsing it into 1933 to 1945. The building is a genuine work in its own right and the Holocaust Tower is unlike anything else in a museum.
places.what_ruined: The architecture is deliberately disorienting, with slanting floors and dead ends, which some visitors find powerful and others find exhausting. Certain temporary exhibitions are charged despite the free core. It is a heavy visit and there is no light way to do it.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. Admission to the core exhibition is free of charge for everyone, the collection is serious and unsentimental, and Libeskind's building does work that no display case could.

places.name: Topography of Terror
places.headline: Free, Open Until Eight, and the Hardest Hour in Berlin
places.body:
The Topography of Terror is free admission and opens daily 10 am to 8 pm, with the outdoor areas open until nightfall.

It stands on the ground where the Gestapo headquarters, the SS leadership and the Reich Security Main Office stood. The buildings are gone; what remains is the site itself, a surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall along Niederkirchnerstrasse, and an exhibition that does something unusual and uncomfortable.

Most Holocaust memorials document what was done to people. This one documents who did it: the administrators, the desk officers, the career police officials, with names, photographs and biographies. It is the institutional machinery examined at close range, and it is harder to walk away from than a memorial.
places.what_great: Free admission and open until 8 pm, which is later than almost any museum in the city and makes it possible after a full day. It examines perpetrators rather than only victims, which is rare and important. A long surviving section of the Berlin Wall runs along the site boundary at no cost.
places.what_ruined: It is relentless, text-heavy and takes concentration, and there is no light way through it. The indoor exhibition is a single dense hall that gets crowded in bad weather. The outdoor trench exhibition is exposed, so a wet or cold day materially changes the visit.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. It is free, it is open late, and it does something no other Berlin site does: it examines the perpetrators rather than only commemorating the victims.

places.name: Book of Kells Experience at Trinity College
places.headline: Twenty-Six Euros for a Ninth-Century Manuscript and the Room It Lives In
places.body:
The Book of Kells Experience at Trinity College starts at 26 euros per person, and the standard visit runs about 90 minutes.

It is worth being precise about what you see, because this is where expectations go wrong. The Book of Kells is displayed as two open pages under glass, and you file past them. The manuscript is astonishing and the display is necessarily brief. What most visitors remember instead is the Long Room, the barrel-vaulted eighteenth-century library upstairs, which is one of the most photographed interiors in Europe and deserves it.

Trinity students and staff visit free of charge and can bring up to two guests, which is worth knowing if you have any connection to the college.
places.what_great: The Long Room is spectacular and justifies the ticket largely on its own. The digital exhibition around the manuscript does a real job of explaining what you are looking at. Trinity students, staff and alumni go free and can bring up to two guests.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-six euros is steep for what is, at the manuscript itself, a filed-past view of two pages. The route is one-way and paced by the group. The college is in the middle of Dublin and the surrounding streets are among the busiest in the city, so arriving is rarely calm.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the Long Room is genuinely one of the great library interiors and the manuscript is extraordinary. Value is three: 26 euros is a lot when the manuscript itself is two open pages behind glass.
places.meta_description: The Book of Kells Experience starts at 26 euros per person. What you actually see, why the Long Room matters more, and how to time it.

places.practical: Book a timed slot in advance, since this is among the busiest paid attractions in Ireland. Early slots are calmer. Give the Long Room more of your time than the manuscript, which is the reverse of what most people plan.

places.name: EPIC The Irish Emigration Museum
places.headline: Twenty-Two Online, Twenty-Four at the Door, and No Objects At All
places.body:
EPIC charges 22.00 euros for an adult aged 18 to 64 booking online and 24.00 on the day, with teenagers aged 13 to 17 at 15.00 online and 16.00 on the day.

The thing to understand before buying is that EPIC has no collection. It is a fully digital museum in the vaults of the CHQ building, telling the story of Irish emigration through twenty rooms of screens, projections and interactive galleries. There are no objects.

That is either the appeal or the problem, and which one it is for you is worth deciding in advance. It handles a diffuse, unphotogenic subject, thirty million people leaving over three centuries, better than an artefact museum could. But visitors expecting a traditional museum sometimes feel they have paid 22 euros for a very good exhibition rather than a collection.
places.what_great: It solves a genuinely hard problem: how to tell the story of emigration when the evidence is scattered across the world. The genealogy element lets Irish-descended visitors look up their own family, which is the part people remember. Booking online saves 2 euros and teenagers pay 15.
places.what_ruined: There are no objects at all, which disappoints anyone expecting a conventional museum. Twenty-two euros is a lot for a screen-based experience in a city with several free national museums. Walk-up costs 2 euros more than booking ahead for exactly the same visit.
places.rating_rationale: Four because it does something genuinely difficult well: tell a diaspora story with almost no artefacts. Value is four, with online booking two euros cheaper and real family rates.

places.name: National Museum of Scotland
places.headline: Free Entry in a City That Charges for Almost Everything Else
places.body:
The National Museum of Scotland has free entry, with charges for some special exhibitions only. In a city where the castle, the underground tours and most of the Royal Mile attractions all charge, that single fact makes this the best-value few hours in Edinburgh.

The collection is unusually broad: Scottish history and archaeology in one wing, natural history, world cultures, science and technology in another, joined by a Victorian glass-roofed grand gallery that is worth standing in on its own.

The roof terrace is the part visitors miss. It is free, it is at the top of the building, and it gives a view over the Old Town rooftops to the castle that many people pay for elsewhere.
places.what_great: Free entry to a genuinely national-scale collection, which in Edinburgh is close to unique. The range means it works for almost anyone, including families on a wet afternoon. The roof terrace view over the Old Town costs nothing and is one of the best in the city.
places.what_ruined: It is large and the layout across old and new buildings confuses people, so first visits often involve backtracking. Special exhibitions are charged, which is a jolt inside a free museum. It is one of the busiest indoor spaces in Edinburgh during festival season and in bad weather.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. Entry is free, the collection ranges from Scottish history to natural science to technology, and the roof terrace gives one of the best free views in Edinburgh.

places.name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
places.headline: Twenty-Two in Advance, Twenty-Six at the Door, and Mary Queen of Scots' Bedchamber
places.body:
The Palace of Holyroodhouse charges 22.00 pounds for an adult booking in advance and 26.00 pounds on the day. Young people aged 18 to 24 pay 14.00 in advance and 17.00 on the day, children aged 5 to 17 pay 11.00 and 13.00, disabled visitors pay the same rates as children, an access companion goes free and under 5s are free.

The palace is the King's official residence in Scotland, at the bottom of the Royal Mile with Arthur's Seat rising behind it. The part most people come for is the historic apartments: Mary Queen of Scots' chambers, including the small room where her secretary David Rizzio was murdered in 1566 in front of her while she was six months pregnant.

The ruined abbey in the grounds is the quieter surprise and is included in the ticket.
places.what_great: Mary Queen of Scots' apartments are the real thing rather than a reconstruction, and the Rizzio murder room lands harder in person than any retelling. The ruined abbey is included and is often empty. Booking ahead saves 4 pounds a head, and an access companion goes free.
places.what_ruined: Turning up without booking costs 4 pounds more per adult for exactly the same visit. The route is fixed and one-way, so you cannot linger where you want to. The palace closes to visitors entirely during royal visits, which is not always obvious when planning.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the historical apartments and the abbey ruins are genuinely strong, held back by a fixed route and a price that jumps if you do not book. Value is four: booking ahead saves 4 pounds and children pay 11.

places.name: Kinkaku-ji
places.headline: Five Hundred Yen for One of the Best Views in Japan, and You Cannot Linger
places.body:
Kinkaku-ji is the rare famous thing that is not overpriced. General admission is 500 yen, primary and middle school students pay 300 yen, and the temple is open 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. all year round. Against Kyoto's 2026 cost of visiting, where the top band of the city lodging tax is 10,000 yen per person per night, a 500 yen ticket to the Golden Pavilion is close to the best value in the city.

What the price does not buy is time with it. The route through the grounds is a one-way loop and the pavilion is viewed from across the Mirror Pond rather than entered. The honest description is a walk of twenty to thirty minutes with one spectacular sightline near the start, which is where every other visitor is also standing.

Plan it as one stop rather than the day. The 9:00 opening is the single best lever you have.
places.what_great: Five hundred yen, open every day of the year, and no reservation system to navigate. The gold leaf reflected in the Mirror Pond is a genuinely singular sight and the grounds are immaculately kept. For a city that has spent 2026 adding costs to visitors, this is one of the few headline attractions that has not moved its price out of reach.
places.what_ruined: You cannot go inside the pavilion, and the loop is one-way, so if the main viewpoint is packed you cannot circle back and wait it out. The whole visit is short enough that people who cross the city for it alone often feel shortchanged. It is in the far north-west, so it costs you a bus ride each way.
places.rating_rationale: Four rather than five because the visit is short, one-way and viewed at a distance, which is a real limitation rather than a matter of taste. Value is five: 500 yen is exceptional for a site of this stature in a city that has spent 2026 raising the cost of visiting.

places.why_go: For one specific view: the gold pavilion reflected in the Mirror Pond, which is among the most recognisable images in Japan and considerably better in person than in photographs.

places.skip_if: You have one day in Kyoto and want depth rather than an icon, in which case Fushimi Inari or the Higashiyama temples give you considerably more time on your feet for your money.
places.practical: Be there at 9:00. The pond view faces the crowd bottleneck and the pavilion catches morning light well. Combine it with Ryoan-ji and Ninna-ji, which are close by on the same side of the city, otherwise you are spending most of the trip on a bus for a half-hour visit.

places.name: Nijo Castle
places.headline: Eight Hundred Yen for the Floors That Were Built to Betray You
places.body:
Nijo Castle charges 800 yen for a castle admission ticket, with 400 yen for junior and senior high school students and 300 yen for elementary school students. Entry is free of charge for those under elementary school age.

What makes it worth the trip is the Ninomaru Palace, and specifically its floors. They are built to chirp underfoot, the so-called nightingale floors, as a security measure against anyone approaching unheard. You walk the whole palace on them, and the sound follows you room to room.

The painted screens inside are originals or high-quality reproductions depending on the room, and the rooms themselves are arranged by rank, so the further in you get the more restricted the access historically was. It is the clearest surviving illustration of how Tokugawa power was staged.
places.what_great: Eight hundred yen for a UNESCO World Heritage site with intact palace interiors is exceptional value, particularly in a city that put its lodging tax up to 10,000 yen a night at the top band in 2026. The nightingale floors are a genuine physical experience rather than a display, and the grounds and gardens are included.
places.what_ruined: The Ninomaru Palace interior is a single one-way route in socks with no photography permitted, so it moves at the pace of the group. The Honmaru Palace requires a separate advance reservation and its own ticket. Coach tours arrive in waves and the palace corridors do not absorb them well.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. The nightingale floors and the Ninomaru palace interiors are unlike anything else in Kyoto, and at 800 yen it is one of the best-value major sites in a city that has been raising prices everywhere else.

places.why_go: For the Ninomaru Palace, which is one of the few places you can walk through intact shogunate-era state rooms, and for the floors, which are an engineering answer to assassination that you experience with your feet.
places.the_good: Eight hundred yen for a World Heritage site with intact interiors. The nightingale floors work exactly as described. School-age rates are genuinely cheap and under-school-age children are free. The gardens are included and are worth the extra twenty minutes.
places.the_downsides: The palace route is one-way, in socks, with no photography, and you move at the speed of whoever is in front of you. The Honmaru Palace is a separate ticket needing advance reservation. Tour coaches concentrate through the middle of the day.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in Japanese history or architecture, families given the cheap child rates, and travellers who want a major Kyoto site that has not priced itself out of reach.
places.skip_if: You have one day in Kyoto and want temples and gardens rather than political history, in which case Fushimi Inari and the Higashiyama walk give you more. Skip the Honmaru add-on unless you have booked it in advance.
places.practical: Go at opening or in the last ninety minutes to miss the coach groups. Wear socks you are happy to walk a palace in, since shoes come off for the Ninomaru route. If you want the Honmaru Palace, reserve it in advance; it cannot be added on arrival.

places.verdict: The best-value major site in Kyoto and the one that best explains how the country was actually governed. Go early, take the gardens as well as the palace, and reserve the Honmaru separately if you want it.

places.name: Oceanario de Lisboa
places.headline: Twenty-Nine Euros at Opening, Twenty-Seven at Midday, and Under-Threes Free
places.body:
The Oceanario prices by time slot, which is unusual and worth understanding before you book. For the 10 am to 11:30 am slot, ages 0 to 2 are free, 3 to 12 year olds pay 17 euros, 13 to 64 year olds pay 29 euros and over-65s pay 19 euros. From 12 pm to 3:30 pm the same tiers drop to 16, 27 and 18 euros.

So the busiest slot is also the most expensive one, and going a couple of hours later is both cheaper and quieter. That is the opposite of how most attractions work and most visitors do not notice it.

The building itself sits out in the marina at Parque das Nacoes, reached by a walkway over the water. The design centres on one enormous tank, viewed from two levels, with four separate habitat displays arranged around it so that the central ocean is always visible through them. It reads as one continuous ocean rather than a series of boxes, and it is the reason this aquarium is regularly rated the best in Europe.
places.what_great: The central-tank design is genuinely clever and holds attention far longer than a conventional aquarium. Under-3s go free and the midday slot is 2 euros cheaper per adult than the opening one. Parque das Nacoes around it is pleasant, modern and easy to walk with children.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-nine euros for an adult at the opening slot makes a family visit expensive. It is out at Parque das Nacoes, well away from central Lisbon, so it costs a metro trip each way. Weekends and school holidays are very busy regardless of which slot you pick.
places.rating_rationale: Five because it is one of the best-designed public aquariums in the world and the central tank genuinely works. Value is four: 29 euros is a lot for a family, though the tiered time slots and free under-threes soften it.

places.name: Buckingham Palace State Rooms
places.headline: Thirty-Three Pounds in Advance, Thirty-Seven on the Day, and One Pound on Universal Credit
places.body:
The State Rooms at Buckingham Palace charge 33.00 pounds for an adult booking in advance and 37.00 pounds on the day. Young people aged 18 to 24 pay 21.50 in advance and 24.50 on the day.

The detail worth knowing, and one that is not widely advertised, is that 1 pound tickets are available to people on Universal Credit and other named UK benefits. That is a serious concession on an otherwise expensive ticket and it applies to the same visit.

The State Rooms are the working ceremonial heart of the palace, used for official entertaining, and they are open to visitors only during limited periods of the year. That scarcity is part of what you are paying for.
places.what_great: The rooms are genuinely on the scale the building implies, and they are the ones actually used for state occasions rather than a reconstruction. Booking in advance saves 4 pounds a head. The 1 pound benefits ticket is a real and unusually generous concession.
places.what_ruined: Thirty-three pounds is expensive and 37 on the day punishes spontaneity. Opening is seasonal, so the visit is unavailable for much of the year. The route is fixed and busy, and photography is restricted inside the State Rooms.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the State Rooms are genuinely grand and open only part of the year, which makes the visit feel earned. Value is three: 33 pounds in advance is a lot, and rises to 37 if you turn up without booking.

places.name: Natural History Museum
places.headline: Free, Enormous, and Best Visited in the Last Two Hours of the Day
places.body:
The Natural History Museum is free, and that single fact changes how you should plan it. There is no ticket to justify, so there is no reason to try to see everything, and no reason not to come twice.

The museum offers free entry tickets you can book in advance, which is the practical lever: booked ticket holders skip the general queue. On a wet weekend in school holidays that queue is the entire difference between a good visit and an hour on the pavement.

The building itself, Waterhouse's terracotta cathedral of a museum, is the thing many people remember longest. The main hall is worth ten minutes and is where almost everybody stalls; the galleries beyond it empty out considerably.
places.what_great: It costs nothing, which makes a short focused visit completely guilt-free. Free entry tickets let you skip the queue. The architecture is a genuine attraction in its own right, and the mineral and meteorite galleries are consistently quiet while the crowd is downstairs.
places.what_ruined: The queue without a booked ticket can be long and is entirely avoidable, which makes it more annoying. The main hall and the dinosaur gallery are the two most crowded rooms in the museum and are the two everybody heads for first. Paid special exhibitions sit inside a free museum, which is a jarring transition.
places.rating_rationale: Five across the board. It is free, the building alone justifies the trip, and the only real cost is crowding, which is a scheduling problem rather than a value problem.

places.what_it_is: A national museum of natural history in South Kensington, housed in an 1881 Waterhouse building, covering life and earth sciences from dinosaurs and mammals to minerals, meteorites and human origins.
places.why_go: Because it is one of the great free museums anywhere, and because the building is as much the point as the collection. Very few museums of this quality cost nothing to enter.
places.the_good: Free entry, free bookable tickets that bypass the queue, and enough range that a repeat visit finds new things. Members get free entry to the paid exhibitions and can skip queues. The quieter upper galleries are genuinely peaceful even on busy days.
places.the_downsides: Without a booked ticket the entry queue can be substantial. The main hall and dinosaurs are heavily congested, which shapes many people's whole impression. Special exhibitions are ticketed separately inside an otherwise free museum.
places.best_for: Families, anyone in London on a budget, repeat visitors who can treat it as a one-hour stop, and people who care about Victorian architecture as much as about the collection.
places.skip_if: You have one day in London and no particular interest in natural history. It is a superb museum but it is not the thing that makes London distinctive, and the Victoria and Albert next door may suit you better.
places.practical: Book a free entry ticket in advance and go straight past the main hall, coming back to it later when the entry surge has moved on. The last two hours of the day are markedly calmer than the middle. South Kensington station connects by tunnel, which matters in the rain.
places.tickets: General admission is free. Free entry tickets can be booked in advance and let you skip the queue. Special exhibitions are ticketed separately, and members get free entry to them.
places.getting_there: South Kensington on the Circle, District and Piccadilly lines, with a pedestrian tunnel running from the station to the museums, which is the sensible route in bad weather.
places.location_context: South Kensington, on Exhibition Road alongside the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Science Museum. Three major free museums sit within a few minutes of each other, which makes this the highest-value square mile in London for anyone not spending money.
places.time_needed: Two hours is a good visit. Ninety minutes is enough if you pick two galleries. Because it is free there is no penalty in leaving early and returning another day.
places.accessibility: Step-free access is available and the museum publishes detailed access information; the tunnel route from South Kensington station avoids the street crossing entirely.
places.verdict: One of the best-value attractions in Europe by the simple measure that it costs nothing and is world class. Book the free ticket, skip the main hall crush, and treat it as two short visits rather than one long one.

places.name: St Paul's Cathedral
places.headline: Twenty-Seven Pounds, and the Dome Climb Is the Part You Will Remember
places.body:
St Paul's charges 27 pounds per adult and 10.50 per child for Monday to Saturday sightseeing, with discounts for families and groups. Sunday is a day of worship rather than sightseeing, which catches a lot of visitors out.

The cathedral floor is impressive and the crypt holds Nelson and Wellington, but the thing that makes the ticket worth it is the climb. The Whispering Gallery, then the Stone Gallery, then the Golden Gallery, each higher and each with a better view, ending on an external walkway around the dome with London laid out underneath.

If you cannot or would rather not climb several hundred steps, you are paying full price for perhaps half the experience, and that is worth knowing before you book.
places.what_great: The dome galleries give one of the best views in London and the climb is a genuine experience rather than a lift ride. Wren's interior is magnificent on its own terms, and the crypt is a serious historical stop. Child admission at 10.50 pounds is reasonable, with family and group discounts available.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-seven pounds is steep, and the best part of it is a 528-step climb that excludes a lot of visitors. Sightseeing is Monday to Saturday only, so a Sunday arrival cannot do the paid visit at all. The upper galleries are narrow and can feel uncomfortable when busy.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the dome and the galleries are genuinely memorable and the interior is magnificent. Value is three because 27 pounds is a lot and the best part of it requires 528 steps you may not want to climb.
places.meta_description: St Paul's costs 27 pounds per adult and 10.50 per child for Monday to Saturday sightseeing. Why the dome climb is the part that justifies the ticket.

places.what_it_is: Christopher Wren's cathedral on Ludgate Hill, completed in 1711 after the Great Fire, with a dome that dominated the London skyline for two and a half centuries and three climbable galleries inside and around it.
places.why_go: For the dome climb and the view from the Golden Gallery, and for one of the finest church interiors in Britain. The Whispering Gallery is a genuine acoustic curiosity rather than a marketing line.
places.the_good: The climb is memorable in a way lift-served viewpoints never are, and each of the three galleries is a distinct experience. The crypt holds Nelson, Wellington and Wren himself. The building sits at the foot of the Millennium Bridge, so it combines naturally with Tate Modern across the river.
places.the_downsides: At 27 pounds it is expensive, and the climb that justifies the price is inaccessible to many. Sightseeing does not run on Sundays. The upper stairs are narrow, enclosed and slow when the cathedral is busy, which makes them hard work on a warm day.
places.best_for: Anyone who can manage several hundred steps and wants the best earned view in London, plus visitors interested in Wren, in English naval and military history, or in church architecture.
places.skip_if: You cannot climb stairs comfortably, in which case a large part of the ticket value is unavailable to you. Skip it also if you have already committed to Westminster Abbey and are watching the budget.
places.practical: Go early on a weekday and climb first while your legs are fresh and the stairwells are quiet. Check that your visit is not on a Sunday. Cross the Millennium Bridge to Tate Modern afterwards, which costs nothing and is the best short walk in the city.
places.tickets: Monday to Saturday sightseeing is 27 pounds per adult and 10.50 pounds per child, with discounts for families and groups. Sunday is a day of worship and sightseeing admission does not operate.
places.getting_there: St Paul's on the Central line is directly outside. Mansion House and Blackfriars are both short walks, and the Millennium Bridge connects on foot to Bankside and Tate Modern.
places.location_context: Ludgate Hill in the City of London, the financial district, which means the surrounding streets are busy on weekdays and notably quiet at weekends. The riverside and Bankside are a five-minute walk over the bridge.
places.time_needed: Two hours including the full climb. Around an hour if you stay on the cathedral floor and in the crypt.
places.accessibility: The cathedral floor and crypt are accessible, but the Whispering, Stone and Golden Galleries are reached only by stairs, so the dome section of the visit is not available to everyone.
places.verdict: Worth the money if you are going to climb it, and questionable value if you are not. Book a weekday morning, go up before you look around at ground level, and pair it with the free walk over the Millennium Bridge to Tate Modern.

places.name: Tate Modern
places.headline: Free Entry to a Power Station Full of Modern Art, and the View Is Free Too
places.body:
Tate Modern occupies the former Bankside Power Station, and the building is the reason to go even if the art leaves you cold. Admission to the permanent collection is free, with opening from 10.00 Sunday to Thursday.

The Turbine Hall is the space everyone photographs, a vast former machine room now used for single large commissions. It is free, it takes ten minutes, and it is one of the few genuinely surprising interior spaces in London.

The upper levels give wide views across the Thames to St Paul's, and they also cost nothing. On a clear afternoon that view is competitive with paid viewing platforms elsewhere in the city.
places.what_great: Free admission to the permanent collection, free views over the river, and a building that would be worth visiting empty. Under-11s go free with a parent, 16 to 25-year-olds can join Tate Collective for cheap exhibition tickets, and companions of disabled visitors go free.
places.what_ruined: The permanent collection is uneven and the labelling is often more confident than the work. Paid exhibitions sit inside a free museum. Weekends in the Turbine Hall are extremely crowded, and the layout across two linked buildings confuses almost everyone on a first visit.
places.rating_rationale: Four because modern art divides people and this collection will not convert a sceptic. Value is five without qualification: the permanent collection and the river views cost nothing.
places.meta_description: Tate Modern is free, open Sunday to Thursday from 10.00, and the upper-floor views over the Thames cost nothing at all.

places.what_it_is: A national gallery of international modern and contemporary art on the south bank of the Thames, housed in the converted Bankside Power Station, with the Turbine Hall as its central space.
places.why_go: For the building, for the free river views from the upper floors, and for a collection that covers the twentieth century broadly. The Turbine Hall commissions are frequently the most talked-about art installations in the country.
places.the_good: It is free, it is open late enough on most days to be an evening stop, and the views cost nothing. The Tate Collective scheme gives 16 to 25-year-olds cheap exhibition access. It sits directly on the river walk, so it combines with the Millennium Bridge and St Paul's without any transport.
places.the_downsides: The permanent hang is uneven, and visitors who do not already like modern art rarely leave converted. Special exhibitions are paid, which surprises people in a free museum. The two-building layout is genuinely confusing and the crowding at weekends is severe.
places.best_for: Anyone already interested in modern art, visitors on a budget, people who like industrial architecture, and anyone wanting a free high view over central London.
places.skip_if: Modern and contemporary art actively annoys you. Nothing here will change that, and the National Gallery on the other side of the river is free too and holds work you may prefer.
places.practical: Go on a weekday, enter through the Turbine Hall ramp for the full effect of the space, and go up to the upper levels for the view before you look at any art. Combine it with the Millennium Bridge crossing to St Paul's, which takes five minutes and is the best short walk in central London.
places.tickets: The permanent collection is free. Exhibitions are ticketed, with members getting unlimited free entry. Up to four children aged 11 and under go free per parent or guardian, visitors aged 16 to 25 can join Tate Collective for 5 pound exhibition tickets, and entry for companions of disabled visitors is free.
places.getting_there: Southwark on the Jubilee line and Blackfriars on the Circle and District lines are both short walks. From St Paul's on the Central line, cross the Millennium Bridge on foot.
places.location_context: Bankside, on the south bank of the Thames facing St Paul's Cathedral, on the stretch of riverside walk that runs from the Globe to Borough Market. The immediate area is well served for food and busy in the evenings.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours for the collection and the views. The Turbine Hall alone is a worthwhile fifteen-minute stop if you are passing.
places.accessibility: Entry for companions of disabled visitors is free. The building is served by lifts throughout and the main Turbine Hall entrance is a long step-free ramp.
places.verdict: Worth going for the building and the view even if the art is not your thing, and unbeatable value because both are free. Go on a weekday, take the river view first, and cross the Millennium Bridge afterwards.

places.name: Westminster Abbey
places.headline: Thirty-One Pounds to Walk Through a Thousand Years of English History
places.body:
Westminster Abbey charges 31 pounds for adult sightseeing admission, with over-65s and students at 28 pounds, children aged 6 to 17 at 14 pounds and under-6s free.

That is a lot of money for a church, and the abbey knows it. What you get for it is the coronation church of the English and British monarchy, the burial place of monarchs, and Poets' Corner, which is a denser concentration of literary graves and memorials than anywhere else in the world.

The honest caveat is that the visit is heavily routed. You follow a set path through a crowded building, and the pace is set by the people in front of you. It rewards knowing in advance which three or four things you want to stand in front of.
places.what_great: The building holds a genuinely unmatched concentration of English history, and Poets' Corner alone justifies a long look. Children aged 6 to 17 pay 14 pounds and under-6s are free, and attending a service costs nothing at all, which is the route most people never consider.
places.what_ruined: Thirty-one pounds is a steep admission and the route through is crowded and one-directional, so lingering is difficult. Photography restrictions apply in much of the building. Prices also vary by date, so the figure you are quoted depends on when you go.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the building and what is inside it are extraordinary. Value is three: 31 pounds is among the steepest church admissions in Europe and the visit is tightly routed.

places.what_it_is: A royal church in Westminster, the coronation site of English and British monarchs since 1066, the burial place of many of them, and home to Poets' Corner. It is a working church as well as a visitor attraction.
places.why_go: Because no other single building holds this much of English history in one place. The coronation chair, the royal tombs and Poets' Corner are all inside one route.
places.the_good: The concentration of history is genuinely without equal, the audio guide is included rather than an extra, and there are real child and concession rates. Attending a service is free, which is by far the cheapest way to be inside the building.
places.the_downsides: At 31 pounds it is among the most expensive church admissions in Europe. The visitor route is one-way and crowded, so you move at the speed of the group. Prices shift by date, so the published rate depends on when you look. Photography is restricted through much of the interior.
places.best_for: Anyone with an interest in English history or literature, first-time visitors to London who want one major historic interior, and families who benefit from the 14 pound child rate.
places.skip_if: You are on a budget and have already paid for St Paul's. Two expensive church visits in one trip is a lot, and St Paul's dome climb is the more physically memorable of the two. Also skip the paid visit if you would be content attending a service instead.
places.practical: Book online for a specific time and go early, because the route congests badly by late morning. If cost is the obstacle, check service times and attend one, which is free and puts you inside the same building. Allow more time than you think for Poets' Corner, which is where the visit is actually worth the money.
places.tickets: Published sightseeing prices are 31 pounds for adults and families of one adult and one child, 28 pounds for over-65s and students, 14 pounds for children aged 6 to 17, and free for children aged 0 to 5 and Association members. Prices are published in dated bands, so the exact figure varies with the period of your visit.
places.getting_there: Westminster on the Circle, District and Jubilee lines is a two-minute walk. St James's Park on the Circle and District lines is a similar distance from the other side.
places.location_context: Westminster, directly beside the Houses of Parliament and across from Parliament Square. The area is dense with government buildings and heavy with tour groups, and it is a short walk along the river to the London Eye.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours for the full route with the audio guide. Less if you are moving briskly, but the routing makes it hard to go much faster than the crowd allows.
places.verdict: Extraordinary building, uncomfortable price. Worth it once if English history or literature matters to you, and best experienced early in the day before the route jams. If money is tight, go to a service instead and see the same interior for nothing.

places.name: Alte Pinakothek
places.headline: Nine Euros Most Days and One Euro on Sunday, Which Is Almost Absurd
places.body:
The Alte Pinakothek charges 9 euro regular admission and 6 euro reduced, and on Sundays it is 1 euro. Admission is free for children and young people under the age of 18.

The Sunday rate is not a promotion. It is a standing Bavarian policy across the state collections, and it means one of the world's great holdings of European painting from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century costs about the same as a coffee.

The collection's strengths are Old German and Early Netherlandish painting, Rubens at a depth found nowhere else, and Italian work from the Renaissance. It is the sort of museum where the second-rank rooms in most galleries would be the highlight.
places.what_great: Nine euro regular admission is remarkable for a collection of this standing, and the 1 euro Sunday rate is close to absurd. Under-18s go free. The Rubens holdings in particular are unmatched, and the building is calm and well lit for looking at paintings.
places.what_ruined: The 1 euro Sunday is well known locally, so Sundays are correspondingly busy. Closed Mondays, which catches visitors out. The building sits in a museum quarter rather than a lively part of the city, so there is little around it.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. The collection is one of the most important holdings of old master painting in the world, regular admission is 9 euro, and on Sundays it is 1 euro.
