places.name: Pinakothek der Moderne
places.headline: Ten Euros, One Euro on Sunday, and Four Museums Under One Roof
places.body:
The Pinakothek der Moderne charges 10 euro admission with 7 euro reduced, and 1 euro on Sundays. Children and young people under 18 receive free admission.

The Sunday rate is standing Bavarian policy across the state collections rather than a promotion, and it applies here exactly as it does at the Alte Pinakothek across the square.

What makes this building unusual is that it houses four separate institutions: the modern art collection, the Neue Sammlung design museum, the architecture museum of the Technical University, and the state collection of works on paper. The design museum in the basement is the one most visitors underestimate and the one most of them end up talking about afterwards, because it covers everything from Bauhaus furniture to industrial design and a genuinely serious car collection.
places.what_great: Ten euro for four museums, dropping to 1 euro on Sundays, with under-18s free. The Neue Sammlung design collection is world class and consistently surprises people who came for the paintings. The Stephan Braunfels rotunda is a fine piece of museum architecture in its own right.
places.what_ruined: Four institutions under one roof means uneven signage and visitors missing whole sections, particularly the basement design museum. Closed Mondays. Sundays are busy for the obvious reason. The Kunstareal district around it is institutional and quiet, with little to do outside the museums.
places.rating_rationale: Four because combining four collections in one building is a strength and a scheduling problem in equal measure. Value is five: 10 euro standard, 1 euro on Sundays, free under 18.

places.name: Empire State Building
places.headline: Forty-Four Dollars Before the Booking Fee, and the Best Reason to Go Is What You Can See
places.body:
Empire State Building tickets start at 44 dollars for the 86th-floor main deck, and a 5 dollar booking charge is added to each transaction, so the real floor is 49 dollars before you have chosen anything.

The counterintuitive argument for coming here rather than a taller, newer observatory is simple: this is the building everyone else is looking at. From One World Observatory or Top of the Rock you get a fine view that happens to contain the Empire State Building. From the Empire State Building you get a view that does not, which matters less than people expect, because what the 86th floor actually offers is an open-air deck in the middle of Midtown at a height where the street grid is still legible.

The 102nd floor is enclosed, higher and costs more. Most people are better served staying at 86.
places.what_great: The 86th-floor deck is open-air, which no enclosed observatory can match: you hear the city as well as see it. Its position mid-island means both downtown and uptown are in view at once. Flexible ticket types allow rescheduling, which is genuinely useful given how much the weather decides here.

places.name: New York Botanical Garden
places.headline: Thirty-Five Dollars, Free to New Yorkers on Wednesdays, and Worth the Train
places.body:
The New York Botanical Garden charges a weekday adult all-garden pass of 35 dollars, with 31 for seniors and students and 15 for children. Children under 2 are no charge. On Wednesdays, grounds admission is free to New York City residents all day.

The garden is 250 acres in the Bronx, which is a scale New Yorkers rarely encounter. Inside it is the Enid A. Haupt Conservatory, a Victorian-style glasshouse from 1902, and a fifty-acre stand of old-growth forest that has never been logged, the last remnant of the woodland that covered the whole city.

That forest is the argument for coming. Everything else here exists elsewhere; a never-logged New York forest does not.
places.what_great: Two hundred and fifty acres and a fifty-acre old-growth forest, which is unlike anything else reachable on a Metro-North ticket. The 1902 conservatory is a serious piece of Victorian glasshouse architecture. Free grounds admission for NYC residents on Wednesdays, and children under 2 are no charge.
places.what_ruined: Thirty-five dollars for a weekday adult is steep next to Central Park, which is free. It is in the Bronx, so it costs a train ride and most of a day. The all-garden pass and grounds-only admission are different products and the difference is easy to miss when booking.
places.rating_rationale: Four because 250 acres with a Victorian glasshouse and old-growth forest is a genuinely different New York day. Value is three: 35 dollars on a weekday is a lot unless you are a city resident going on a Wednesday, when the grounds are free.
places.meta_description: The New York Botanical Garden costs 35 dollars weekday adult, and grounds admission is free to NYC residents on Wednesdays.

places.name: One World Observatory
places.headline: The Highest View in the City, Behind Glass, Starting at Forty-Four Dollars
places.body:
One World Observatory sits at the top of One World Trade Center and is the highest view in New York. Standard general admission starts at 44 dollars, a combination ticket at 54, the all-inclusive experience at 64 and a VIP tour at 74.

That ladder is the defining feature of the visit. Where the Empire State Building sells you a deck, this sells you a tiered experience, and the difference between the tiers is largely about queueing and extras rather than about the view, which is identical from all of them.

The view is entirely behind glass. That is a genuine trade against the Empire State Building's open-air 86th floor, and it is the single thing most likely to decide which one you should pick.
places.what_great: It is the highest view in the city and the glass is floor to ceiling, so the outlook is uninterrupted. The harbour, the Statue of Liberty and the Brooklyn and Manhattan bridges all sit in one sweep, which no Midtown observatory can offer. Security and crowd handling are efficient.
places.what_ruined: Everything is behind glass, so there is no open-air option at any price. The four-tier ticket ladder from 44 to 74 dollars makes the real cost hard to pin down before you start. The lift presentation and the routing through retail make it feel like a produced attraction rather than a viewpoint.
places.rating_rationale: Three because it is a very high view delivered as a managed experience, with a scripted lift ride and a route that pushes you through upsells. Value is three: the entry price matches the Empire State Building for a view that is higher but enclosed.
places.meta_description: One World Observatory starts at 44 dollars, rising to 74 for the VIP tier. What the higher tiers actually add and whether the height is worth it.

places.name: Whitney Museum of American Art
places.headline: Free If You Are Twenty-Five or Under, Which Changes the Whole Calculation
places.body:
The Whitney charges 30 dollars for adults and 24 for seniors and students, and is free for visitors aged 25 and under. There are also free Friday nights and free second Sundays.

That pricing structure is the most interesting thing about visiting. New York museums are expensive and most of the concessions are token; here the under-26 rate is not a discount, it is free entry, which makes this the single best-value serious museum in the city for anyone young enough to qualify.

The museum itself is American art from roughly 1900 onward, in a Renzo Piano building at the foot of the High Line with outdoor terraces on several floors. Those terraces are a real part of the visit rather than an afterthought.
places.what_great: Free for everyone 25 and under, plus free Friday nights and free second Sundays, which is genuinely unusual in New York. The building's outdoor terraces give river and skyline views included in the ticket. It is a manageable size, so you can see the whole thing without the exhaustion the larger museums produce.
places.what_ruined: Thirty dollars is a lot if you are 26 or over and do not qualify for any of the free routes. The collection is narrow by design, so if American twentieth-century art is not your interest there is little else. Free Friday nights are correspondingly busy.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the collection and the building are both strong without being overwhelming. Value is four because 30 dollars is standard for New York but the free access for 25 and under, on Friday nights and on second Sundays is unusually generous.
places.meta_description: The Whitney costs 30 dollars, 24 for seniors and students, and is free if you are 25 or under. Free Friday nights and second Sundays too.

places.name: Eiffel Tower
places.headline: The Ticket You Choose Matters More Than the Tower
places.body:
The Eiffel Tower is the one Paris sight where a good visit and a wasted afternoon are decided before you arrive, at the moment you pick a ticket type and a time slot.

Official adult pricing is 23,50 euros for the second floor by lift and 36,70 euros for the summit by lift. Youth aged 12 to 24 pay 11,80 and 18,40, children aged 4 to 11 and disabled visitors pay 6,00 and 9,20, and under 4s are free. The stairs are the quiet bargain: the same second floor on foot is 14,80 euros for an adult.

What you are buying is height and one specific view, which is the view of Paris that does not have the Eiffel Tower in it. That is the old joke and it is also the honest reason to consider Montparnasse instead if a photograph is the point.
places.what_great: The second-floor view is the genuinely great one, close enough that the city reads as streets and roofs rather than a map. The youth band runs all the way to 24 and under-4s are free, which is unusually generous for a landmark this size. The stair ticket at 14,80 euros is both cheaper and usually faster than the lift queue.
places.what_ruined: The summit costs 13,20 euros more than the second floor for a view that is further away and more crowded, and it is first to close in high wind. Resellers outrank the official site and charge more for the identical timed slot. The Champ de Mars approach is worked hard by bracelet and petition scammers.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the second-floor view genuinely earns it. Value is three: 23,50 euros to the second floor is fair, 36,70 to the summit is a lot for a more distant version of the same city.
places.meta_description: Eiffel Tower tickets run 23,50 euros to the second floor and 36,70 to the summit. What each buys, why the stairs win, and when to skip the summit.

places.what_it_is: A 330-metre iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars, built for the 1889 World's Fair and kept afterwards because taking it down proved less useful than leaving it up. There are three visitor levels: first floor, second floor and the summit.
places.why_go: Because it is the fixed point of the city, and because the second-floor view is the clearest reading of how Paris is actually laid out. From up there the Haussmann boulevards stop being a history-book phrase and become a visible pattern.
places.the_good: The engineering is legible from underneath in a way photographs never convey, and standing under the base costs nothing. The ticket tiers are published plainly, the youth band is wide, and the stair option is a real saving rather than a token one.
places.the_downsides: Timed slots sell out, and the summit closes in high wind with no warning. The base is a working ground for bracelet scammers, fake petitioners and unlicensed sellers. Reseller sites dominate search results and charge above the official rate for the same ticket.
places.best_for: First-time visitors to Paris, families with children under 12 given the low child rates, and anyone who wants one high view and is happy for it to be this one.
places.skip_if: You mainly want a skyline photograph with the tower in it, in which case Montparnasse does the job better. Skip the summit specifically if you are watching money: the second floor is the better view and 13,20 euros cheaper.
places.practical: Book an exact time slot on the official site, not a reseller. If the lift queue is long and you are able-bodied, buy the stair ticket: 14,80 euros, a shorter queue, and a climb most people manage comfortably. Ignore anyone approaching you with a clipboard or a loop of string.

places.getting_there: Bir-Hakeim on Metro line 6 and Trocadero on lines 6 and 9 are closest, with RER C at Champ de Mars-Tour Eiffel. Trocadero is the approach worth taking on foot because it delivers the tower head-on across the river.
places.location_context: The 7th arrondissement, on the Left Bank at the end of the Champ de Mars, with the Trocadero gardens across the Seine. It is a formal, expensive, largely residential quarter, and the restaurants nearest the base are priced for people who are not coming back.
places.time_needed: Two to three hours including security and queueing for a second-floor visit, nearer four for the summit. Seeing it from underneath and from Trocadero takes about an hour and costs nothing.
places.accessibility: Lifts serve the first and second floors, and disabled visitors pay the child rate of 6,00 euros to the second floor and 9,20 to the summit. Summit access is more limited because the upper lift is smaller.
places.verdict: Go, take the second floor, and skip the summit unless the extra height genuinely matters to you. Everything people hate about this visit is a queueing and pricing problem rather than a problem with the tower, and both are solved by booking the right ticket direct.

places.name: Louvre Museum
places.headline: Now Charges Non-Europeans Ten Euros More, and Still Cannot Be Done in a Day
places.body:
The Louvre's pricing works in a way that matters to most people reading this. General admission is 22,00 euros for residents and citizens of the European Economic Area and 32,00 euros for everyone else, published as a two-tier rate on the museum's own site.

That is a meaningful gap and it is better known before you arrive than at the desk. Under 18s and EEA residents under 26 have their own free and reduced categories.

The other thing worth knowing is that the building defeats people. This is a former royal palace's worth of galleries, and the standard mistake is treating it as a checklist. The Mona Lisa is a long shuffle for a short look at a small painting behind glass across a crowded room, and it is the least rewarding famous thing in the building.
places.what_great: The collection is without equal in range, from Mesopotamia to the mid-nineteenth century, and the building is a large part of the visit. Under 18s and EEA residents under 26 get in free or reduced. The Near Eastern antiquities and the French sculpture courts are near-empty while the crowd concentrates on three or four paintings.
places.what_ruined: Non-EEA visitors pay 32,00 euros against 22,00 for EEA visitors, a ten-euro gap based on where you are from rather than what you see. The Mona Lisa room is the worst-value twenty minutes in Paris. Signage is poor for a building this size, and unplanned visits reliably become three hours of walking and very little looking.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the collection, which has no real rival. Value is three because a non-EEA adult pays 32,00 euros and because the building's scale means most visitors see a fraction of what they paid for.
places.meta_description: The Louvre charges 22 euros to EEA visitors and 32 to everyone else. What that two-tier price buys, and how to use the museum without wasting it.

places.name: Pantheon
places.headline: Sixteen Euros, Free Under Twenty-Six, and Foucault's Pendulum Still Swings
places.body:
The Pantheon charges 16 euros, with free admission for under 26-year-old residents of the EU.

Three things are worth your time inside. The nave holds a working replica of Foucault's pendulum, the 1851 experiment that demonstrated the rotation of the Earth in front of an audience, and it still swings. The crypt below holds Voltaire, Rousseau, Hugo, Zola, the Curies and Josephine Baker, which is the French republic deciding in public who it wants to have been. And in season there is a dome colonnade you can climb for one of the better views over the Left Bank.

It is a colder building than Sainte-Chapelle a mile north, and deliberately so. This is the republic's answer to a cathedral.
places.what_great: The pendulum is a genuine scientific artefact rather than a display, and watching it move is oddly affecting. The crypt is a direct statement of national values, argued over for two centuries and still being added to. Under-26 EU residents get in free, and the dome climb in season is one of the best paid views in Paris.
places.what_ruined: The main space is enormous, cold and largely empty, which some visitors find impressive and others find a waste of sixteen euros. The dome climb is seasonal and closes in bad weather. The crypt is dimly lit and the labelling assumes you already know who these people were.
places.rating_rationale: Four because it combines a serious neoclassical interior, the crypt of the French republic's chosen dead, and a working physics demonstration. Value is four: 16 euros is fair and under-26 EU residents get in free.

places.the_downsides: The nave is vast and sparse, and at 16 euros some visitors feel they have paid to stand in a cold empty room. The dome is seasonal and weather-dependent. Crypt labelling is thin if French history is not already familiar to you.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in the French Revolution or the Third Republic, visitors with an interest in the history of science, and under-26 EU residents who get in free.
places.skip_if: You want warmth, colour and decoration, in which case Sainte-Chapelle is the better sixteen-to-twenty-two euros. Skip the dome specifically if it is out of season or the weather is poor.
places.practical: Check whether the dome colonnade is open before you go, since it is seasonal and is the best part when available. Go to the crypt first while you have energy for the reading. The Luxembourg gardens are two minutes away and free, which is the natural pairing.
places.tickets: Admission is 16 euros, with free admission for under 26-year-old residents of the EU. The dome colonnade is seasonal and may require a separate timed booking.
places.getting_there: RER B to Luxembourg is the closest station. Cardinal Lemoine and Maubert-Mutualite on Metro line 10 are both a short walk.

places.name: Sainte-Chapelle
places.headline: Twenty-Two Euros for One Room, and Worth It on a Bright Day
places.body:
Sainte-Chapelle is a small building with one overwhelming feature: an upper chapel walled almost entirely in thirteenth-century stained glass. Admission is 22 euros, with free admission for under 26-year-old residents of the EU.

That is a high price for what is, in floor area, one room. It is also close to unarguable on a bright day, because what you are paying for is a light effect no photograph reproduces and very few buildings anywhere can offer.

The corollary is the honest warning. On a grey Paris afternoon the same 22 euros buys a considerably duller experience. This is the rare attraction where checking the forecast is a practical booking decision rather than fussiness.
places.what_great: The upper chapel is genuinely singular, and because the building is small you are not paying for corridors you will not walk. Under-26 EU residents get in free. It sits on the Ile de la Cite within minutes of Notre-Dame and the Conciergerie, so it slots into a day without a special journey.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-two euros for one room is steep, and the payoff depends on sunlight, which the ticket page does not warn you about. The chapel is small enough that one tour group changes the experience. Security is airport-style because the site shares a perimeter with a working courthouse.
places.rating_rationale: Five because the upper chapel is one of the most extraordinary interiors in Europe. Value is four rather than five only because 22 euros for a single room needs the right weather to pay off.
places.meta_description: Sainte-Chapelle costs 22 euros and is essentially one room of thirteenth-century stained glass. Why the weather decides whether it is worth the ticket.

places.name: Vasa Museum
places.headline: Two Hundred and Forty Krona for a Warship That Sank After Twenty Minutes
places.body:
The Vasa Museum charges 240 SEK for an adult, with a combination ticket including the Vrak museum at 359 SEK, and free admission for 0 to 18 year olds.

The Vasa was the pride of the Swedish navy and it sank on its maiden voyage in 1628, about twenty minutes after leaving the dock, in full view of the crowd that had come to watch it depart. It was too narrow, too tall and too heavily armed, and the first serious gust put water through the open gunports.

It then sat in the cold, brackish, low-oxygen water of Stockholm harbour for 333 years, which is exactly the wrong conditions for shipworm and exactly the right ones for oak. Raised in 1961, it is around 98 per cent original timber. Nothing else like it survives anywhere.
places.what_great: A complete seventeenth-century warship, mostly original, standing ten storeys tall indoors. Free for everyone under 18, which makes it genuinely affordable for families. The museum is built around the ship on multiple levels so you see it from keel to rigging.
places.what_ruined: The hall is deliberately dim and humidity-controlled to protect the timber, which makes photography hard and the space feel crowded faster than its size suggests. Two hundred and forty kronor is real money if you are also buying the Vrak combination. It is the busiest museum in Scandinavia in July and August.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. There is no other intact seventeenth-century warship on earth, under-18s are free, and 240 kronor is reasonable for the single most extraordinary object in Scandinavia.
places.meta_description: The Vasa Museum costs 240 SEK for adults and is free for under-18s. A warship raised from the harbour, 98 per cent original.

places.name: Gallerie dell'Accademia
places.headline: Twenty Euros, Two for Young Europeans, and Almost Nobody in It
places.body:
The Gallerie dell'Accademia charges a full price of 20,00 euros, with reduced admission of 2,00 euros for young persons who are EU citizens aged 18 to 25, and free entry for under 18s.

That 2 euro rate is not a typo and it is not a promotion. It is the standard Italian state museum concession, and it makes this one of the cheapest ways in Europe for a young traveller to stand in front of Giorgione, Bellini, Titian, Tintoretto and Veronese in the city where they worked.

The collection is the definitive account of Venetian painting from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century, and it is housed in a former religious complex at the foot of the Accademia bridge. It is also, reliably, the emptiest major attraction in Venice, because the crowd is at San Marco.
places.what_great: The most important collection of Venetian painting anywhere, in the city that produced it. Twenty euros full price and 2 euros for EU citizens aged 18 to 25 is remarkable. It is genuinely quiet compared to everything else in Venice, so you can stand in front of things for as long as you want.
places.what_ruined: Twenty euros is real money if you do not qualify for the concession and are already paying Venice prices for everything else. The labelling is sparse and largely assumes you know the painters. Booking online is through a single authorised operator, which catches people out.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. It holds the definitive collection of Venetian painting, it costs 20 euros, EU citizens aged 18 to 25 pay 2 euros, and it is consistently the quietest major museum in a city drowning in visitors.
places.meta_description: The Gallerie dell'Accademia costs 20 euros, 2 euros for EU citizens aged 18 to 25, and under 18s free. The best-value hour in Venice.

places.name: Hofburg Imperial Palace
places.headline: Twenty Euros for the Sisi Myth, Told Better Than You Expect
places.body:
The Hofburg charges 20,00 euros for adults and 12,00 euros for children from age 6, on fixed admission times, with the standard route running about 60 minutes.

What the ticket buys is three things in sequence: the Imperial Apartments, the Sisi Museum and the Silver Collection. The Sisi Museum is the reason most people come and it is better than its subject matter suggests, because it spends much of its length dismantling the sentimental version of Empress Elisabeth that Austrian tourism otherwise sells hard.

Fixed admission times matter here. This is not a come-when-you-like palace, and turning up without a slot in high season is how people end up eating lunch instead.
places.what_great: The Sisi Museum treats its subject critically rather than as merchandise, which is rare for a national icon. One ticket covers three collections in a single route. Children from six pay 12 euros, and the whole thing takes about an hour, so it fits into a day rather than consuming one.
places.what_ruined: Fixed admission times mean the visit has to be planned around. The route is one-way and busy through the middle of the day. The gift-shop version of Sisi outside the museum flatly contradicts the honest account inside it, which is a strange note to leave on.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the Sisi Museum is unusually honest about the difference between the woman and the legend built on her. Value is four: 20 euros covers three linked attractions and children from six pay 12.

places.name: Kunst Haus Wien
places.headline: Sixteen Euros for the Building Hundertwasser Built to Argue With Straight Lines
places.body:
Kunst Haus Wien charges 16,00 euros for admission, with 13,00 for reduced tickets and for seniors 65 and over. Accompanying persons of people with disabilities receive free admission.

The museum is Hundertwasser's own, built in a converted furniture factory, and it is the clearest place to understand what he was actually arguing for: uneven floors on purpose, no straight lines where he could avoid them, trees growing out of the windows.

It is a short visit and an unusually physical one. You notice the building through your feet before you notice any of the paintings, which is precisely the point he was making.
places.what_great: The building is the argument and you experience it directly rather than reading about it. Sixteen euros is cheap by Vienna museum standards and 13 covers both reduced tickets and over-65s. Accompanying persons of visitors with disabilities go free.
places.what_ruined: It is small, and if Hundertwasser does not interest you there is not much else. The deliberately uneven floors are genuinely awkward for anyone unsteady on their feet. It sits away from the central museum cluster, so it costs a journey.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the building is a genuine one-off and the museum is small enough to enjoy. Value is four: 16 euros is modest for Vienna and the concessions are wide.

places.name: Upper Belvedere
places.headline: Twenty-Three Euros to Stand in Front of The Kiss, and Under-19s Go Free
places.body:
The Upper Belvedere charges 23,00 euros for an admission ticket, 19,00 euros for seniors over 65 and for students under 26, and nothing at all for children and young people under 19.

What almost everybody comes for is Klimt's The Kiss, which hangs here along with the largest collection of his work anywhere. That concentration is both the attraction and the problem: one room absorbs the crowd while a baroque palace full of Austrian art from the medieval period onward sits comparatively quiet around it.

The building is a Baroque summer palace with formal gardens running down to the Lower Belvedere, and the gardens are free to walk. On a good day that walk is a genuine part of the visit rather than a way of getting between two ticket desks.
places.what_great: The Klimt holding is the best anywhere and The Kiss is genuinely worth the trip. Under-19s get in free and the concession rate covers students up to 26. The gardens between Upper and Lower Belvedere are free and are one of the most pleasant walks in central Vienna.
places.what_ruined: The room holding The Kiss is congested for most of the day and people queue to photograph it rather than look at it. The 23 euro ticket covers the Upper Belvedere only, so a full visit to both palaces costs more. The rest of the collection is unfairly overlooked as a result of the Klimt concentration.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the building and the collection are both excellent, held back only by how hard the crowd concentrates on one painting. Value is four: 23 euros is fair, and free entry for everyone under 19 is a real family saving.

places.what_it_is: A Baroque palace on the upper terrace of the Belvedere complex, built for Prince Eugene of Savoy and now a museum of Austrian art holding the world's largest collection of Gustav Klimt paintings, including The Kiss.

places.the_downsides: The Kiss draws a persistent crowd and the room around it is the least comfortable part of the museum. The 23 euro ticket is for the Upper Belvedere alone, so seeing the Lower Belvedere as well means paying again. Much of the rest of the collection goes unlooked-at.
places.best_for: Anyone who wants to see Klimt properly, visitors interested in Baroque architecture, and families given the free under-19 entry.
places.skip_if: You have limited time in Vienna and a broader interest in art history, in which case the Kunsthistorisches Museum covers far more ground. Skip it if crowds around a single famous painting are the thing you most dislike about museums.
